Teie viimasele kirjale soovisime täpsustada järgnevalt, kuid usun, et kohtumine looks parima selguse:

_Sõlmitud hankelepingute muutmisel peab arvestama riigihangete seaduse (edaspidi RHS) § 123 toodut. Vastavalt riigihangete seaduse § 123 lg 1 p 6:_

_(1) Hankijal on õigus sõlmitud hankelepingut muuta uut riigihanget korraldamata, kui:_

# ettevõtja asendatakse osaliselt või täielikult uue ettevõtjaga, kes ei kuuluks kõrvaldamisele käesoleva seaduse § 95 kohaselt ja kes täidab riigihanke alusdokumentides sätestatud kvalifitseerimise tingimusi, ettevõtja restruktureerimise, sealhulgas ülevõtmise, ühinemise, võõrandamise või maksejõuetuse tõttu, eeldusel et ettevõtja asendamisega ei kaasne hankelepingu muid olulisi muudatusi;

 

_Sisuliselt tähendab see, et lepingu poole vahetumisel tuleb uus pakkuja uuesti kvalifitseerida vastavalt riigihanke alusdokumentidele ning kontrollida, et tal ei esineks RHS § 95 toodud kõrvaldamise aluseid. Juhul kui pakkuja ei vasta kvalifitseerimistingimustele ning tal esinevad RHS § 95 toodud kõrvaldamise alused,  ei saa pakkujat vahetada ega lepingut muuta. Kuna see hange on üsna hiljuti tehtud, tekib küsimus, miks kohe ei esitanud pakkumust see ettevõte kes soovib tegelikult teenust osutada ja arveid esitada? Kui selle põhjuseks on asjaolu, et riigihankes pakkumust esitades ei oleks ta (Bolt Operations OÜ) kvalifitseerunud, siis nüüd sellise muudatuse tegemine on samuti välistatud._

Hi [~accountid:61fa31ce845d670071f30e5c], 

The dual currency obligations only relate to customers, not to B2B relations (in Croatia couriers are entrepreneurs or employed by a fleet).

The Act prescribes that traders, from 1.1.2023. until 15.01.2023. (Period of the use of dual currency) must accept payments in cash in HRK and give exchange in EUR or in HRK or both EUR and HRK (if not possible to give it in EUR) 

Therefore, when it comes to couriers and restaurants  - there are no legal rules or obligations on how we should arrange this matter (we just need to allow consumers to pay in both currencies in that period).

Hope this helps, if not, happy to discuss this further. 

BR, 

Iva

The reasoning behind?

* Extra earnings
* Extra orders for the local bonus campaigns
* Easiest way to receive money and doing nothing

Friction points:

* Screwing the algorithm of the machine learning system
* Keeping busy other couriers that are not included in this plan, generating more waiting time for other orders
* Clients are not receiving their orders in time, because sometimes the guilty couriers were waiting for others to come and pickup the order
* Tips is added just for the courier from the parent order, the courier from the child order will not benefit from this feature

Hi [~accountid:62bbfa409e6ba34c99365c7c] [~accountid:6052891960d39e006f72f0f0],

Please find below the external counsel’s feedback on the Omnibus price reductions rules:



_The Omnibus Directive does not impose any specific obligations on marketplaces concerning sales at reduced prices. Regarding marketplaces, the Directive has only reinforced obligations of transparency and complete information to consumers (such as the main parameters determining the ranking of offers, and whether consumers are entering into a contract with a trader or a non-trader)._

 

_Assuming that in Bolt Marketplace:_

* _Bolt is not selling its own products to the consumers_
* _Bolt is acting as an intermediary between traders and consumers for the sale of products_
* _Prices and discounts are fixed and displayed by the traders on the platform_

 

_It is our understanding that the price reduction rules are only applicable to the traders and not to Bolt marketplace insofar traders are the economic operators that are selling the products (via distance-selling)._

 

_That said, in order to avoid legal risks arising from a misconduct from the trader likely to cause harm to consumers,_ +_we recommend to include in the T&Cs for traders_+ _a clause providing that traders are fully aware that they must comply with national and EU rules on price reduction, and that Bolt will not be held liable for traders' failure to comply with such rules; in the event that Bolt is held liable, Bolt is entitled to seek compensation from traders for any damages. We also recommend to prepare a standard message to send to all traders whenever Bolt detects any illegal behaviour regarding the non-compliance with such rules._

 

_We further note that the European Commission has recently proposed one legislative initiative to upgrade rules governing digital services in the EU, the so-called_ *_Digital Services Act (DSA)_*_. This set of rules will apply across the whole EU. The next step will be the adoption of this act by the EU Council, and is expected to enter into force next year. DSA will apply to intermediary services, hosting services and online platforms. It sets out new obligations for online platforms, including consumer information standards._

 

_In general terms, the DSA provides for a general exemption of liability of online platforms, whenever they are intermediaries and do not initiate, select or modify the information that is transmitted by the trader. In relation to hosting services, online platforms are exempt of liability as regards the content of the information whenever they had no knowledge of its illegal content. However, this exemption of liability shall not apply in cases where the online platform initiates, selects or modifies the information (i.e. is not merely transmitting it), or in case the online platform was aware of the illegal content of the information (specially when it comes to information that is being transmitted to consumers within distance contracts with traders) and did not take any actions to remove or disable access to such illegal content._

 

_Considering the requirements of DSA that will soon be adopted as EU regulation,_ +_we recommend Bolt to adopt reporting mechanisms_+ _where any individual can notify the presence on the platform of illegal content (which can relate to the non-compliance with the price reduction rules). The set up of reporting mechanisms is a critical element to minimise or even waive Bolt’s liability with respect to any illegal content in the platform, provided that Bolt reacts by removing such content. We are happy to assist Bolt in engaging and implementing such mechanisms in case you find our assistance is needed._

 

_On a final note, as discussed in our call, we call your attention to the transposition into the national law of Directive (EU) 2019/1937 on the protection of persons who report breaches of EU law (“whistleblowers”). This regime establishes the obligation of companies to implement internal reporting mechanisms allowing people to anonymously report illegal practices._

 

_Finally, please note that if the third assumption indicated above is not verified – i.e. in the event that Bolt modifies the discounts in the context of a Bolt campaign –_ +_then Bolt must comply with the price reduction rules._+

Hi,

Apart from the new changes regarding price reduction (Omnibus provisions - see below), there were no other legislative changes regarding fresh / frozen goods. 

Omnibus provisions:

(1) Any price reduction notice shall indicate the previous price charged by the seller in the same sales area for a specified period before the price reduction is applied. Proof of the previous price will be made through documents submitted by the trader, in this sense, at the request of the authorised staff of the National Authority for Consumer Protection.

(2) The previous price represents the lowest price charged by the seller in the same sales area during the last 30 days before the date of application of the price reduction.

*(3) In the case of products liable to deteriorate or expire rapidly,* the previous price is the lowest price charged by the seller in the same sales area during the last 10 days before the date of application of the price reduction.

Sorina

The only solution to mitigate the costs of the Mems Martin rent until we can terminate the contract is to sublease the premises, since we included a clause whereby we may sublease the premises with the landlord prior consent.

* We made changes to the store and destroyed the interior walls, making it more difficult for the landlord to lease the premises again.

To me, the landlord is not understanding what a sublease is and is thinking that our proposal is to assign our position or terminate the contract instead of subleasing the premises.

[~accountid:620242c0f38765006f6629c7] agreed that later this week he or one of his colleagues will contact the landlord again to better explain our sublease proposal, emphasizing that we are not giving up our position, but that we will continue to be tenants and be responsible to him while we deal with the subtenants.

Let me elaborate on the legal issues we encounter with this approach. In order to mitigate legal risks with this initiative we will need to solve the following legal issues:

* reclassification issues
* privacy issues
* competition law issues

*Reclassification issues*. Given the reclassification risk of drivers, our legal advice on global level has been that we should avoid acceptance rates as metrics for sanctioning the drivers. Monitoring drivers' acceptance rates imposes a high level of control on drivers. High level of control means employment, and reclassifying drivers as employees is something we would like to avoid. To mitigate the risk of reclassification, I would advise on coming up with a business solution in one of the following forms:

* addressing the issue in a form of an incentive, where the driver would be communicated something like ‘_do X, get Y’,_ where X does not equal acceptance rates,
* addressing the issue via certain +objective+ parameters that drivers belonging to Basic category need to fulfil in order to reach certain level. Again, we should avoid making it based on acceptance rates.

*Competition law issues*. As per [~accountid:61addb80b0b630006a695081], this issue has been cleared by external counsels, meaning the risk is practically non-existent. So, greenlight on that issue.

*Privacy issues*. If switch between different categories will take place automatically (without human review), this makes it an automated decision-making which is subject to privacy laws. Having talked to [~accountid:609f85c547ba02006fe1b9c3], I understand that such automation poses a significant risk under privacy laws but I will let [~accountid:609f85c547ba02006fe1b9c3] comment on that in detail.

Hey\! 

Regarding the privacy issue here. 

Such activity likely falls under article 22 of GDPR and constitutes ADM which as a rule is prohibited. The decision to remove the driver from a category based on the acceptance rate significantly effects the data subject (which is the main criteria why this falls under ADM). Once the acceptance rate drops below a level X, driver is excluded from a category which provides more earning opportunities. So if we lower the earning opportunities, then we are affecting someone’s financial circumstances and this is considered a significant effect. Also the idea behind this is to push up driver activity, meaning that we already assume that removing a driver from this category is a significant motivator. 

However, ADM would be allowed under art 22 (2) if the decision would be  necessary for the performance of an agreement. Therefore it would have to be clearly and transparently stated in the agreement with the driver on what are the conditions for the driver to provide their services under a certain category (e.g. acceptance rate has to be X in order to provide services under Y category). 

In addition, the driver would always have the right to contest the decision (removing them from a category) and have a human to review the decision made. 

Liis

In cash heavy markets (Azerbaijan, South Africa, Ghana, Tanzania, Tunisia, Kenya, and Nigeria), reactivation rate (# of reactivated drivers divided by # of churned drivers in the same period) fluctuates between 50-75%. I take the reactivation rate of cash-heavy markets because our top ATI for driver churn is “_I have a question about driver debt_”, which is more prevalent in African and Central Asian markets, but virtually none in European markets.

Assuming this rate applies uniformly across all ticket types (which is a wild guess), more than 50% of churned partners will reactivate.

CS ticket is not a good source for business churn analysis, as:

# In some cases, we can’t really join the business CS ticket with the real business company because of missing information to link those two. In our dashboard, weekly churn of business companies with billing related ticket is < 6 per week.
# Business companies have sales team or account management team that interact with them. Business companies also operate on subscription model, not a typical B2C.

Unless there is a strong business justification, I think it’s better to have a discussion with the sales team instead of doing this ATI analysis.

After some discussion with Jelena and Tanya Parpora I decided to change the scope of this project and to introduce a broader approach. What does it mean?

We (together with Jelena) would create a coaching template for the STLs/TLs that they could use when dealing with issues in their team. * It is not clear what will happen to the existing French and Spanish contracts. *We will need to expressly deal with the amalgamation/termination of the French and Spanish contracts when completing this new contract.* Please agree the intention and we can then look to document the arrangement.
* *Please flag that our teams are reviewing the ‘right to audit clause’ (this is very widely drafted)* ([~accountid:5fa118a781b2880078eb0e6f] / [~accountid:609f85c547ba02006fe1b9c3] for discussion).

+Other points/risks+: 

* We will have no oversight of the reliability and accuracy of the data provided. The data sets should therefore be scrutinised on occasion (to the extent possible) and the arrangement terminated if it is concluded that the data is unreliable. 
* Our logo already features on FoxIntelligence’s website, on the basis that we granted them this right pursuant to the French contract. Data harvesting can be a sensitive issue. There is an opportunity to ask them to remove our logo now if we think the use of it is sensitive.
* After the arrangement has expired Bolt is expected to delete all material data provided by FoxIntelligence that we have downloaded or saved remotely (other than very limited / useless data sets). This is backed up by them having a right to audit our company to check that this has been complied with. If we need to keep a historic track of this data even after the contract expires, we will need to amend this clause. Please flag if there is any intention to store this data after the contract has expired.
* There is no real ability to share the data in any way. Please flag if a right to share data externally is needed.
* I note that our competitor FreeNow also use FoxIntelligence.

*One of the decision that we need to make is: to make comms or not to make comms*

The idea behind “not making comms” to drivers before launching this test is to: (1) minimize PR risk from drivers. However, not sending comms to drivers to inform them that they have higher debt limit may have detrimental effect to the test itself if the basic assumption of driver behavior that I have is proven to be wrong. *My initial assumption is driver will make payment after they get cash-blocked, thus we don’t need to inform the new debt limit* (they will keep on driving anyway until get cash-blocked).

Turns out, my assumption is wrong. Drivers are more strategic and they frequently make payment far before the debt limit is reached. 

This assumption was invalidated using the cash-block log, plus sanity check with Cellulant payment data. The approach to test the assumption looks like this:

# If a payment of a driver is made during the cash-block period, then we label them as “cash-block induced payment”
# All other payments beside (1) is payment made before they got cash-blocked.

Taking data from high-cash markets, we can see that the rate of cash-block induced payment is rather low, around:

# 50% in Kenya
# 40% in Tanzania
# 20% in Azerbaijan, Nigeria, Ghana, and South Africa

Thus, we need to send comms to drivers informing the new debt limit to ensure the validity of the test. However, there is new decision that needs to be made.

# “_Should we inform them that this higher debt limit is part of an experiment?”_
# “_If we conduct a test with higher debt limit and inform them that this is an experiment, will they be disappointed with us if we return their debt limit to normal?”_
# “_If they know this is part of a test, will they be disappointed if in the future we run another test with lower debt limit?”_
## I think this will bring huge disappointment, and will result with bad PR and lower competitive edge against competitors. If we want to bring the debt limit lower, need to properly plan the strategy, analyze competitors, and mitigate risks.
# “_If we inform them the higher debt limit that they have, do we need to inform them about the end date of the test?”_

*Conclusion*

We have three options

||*Option*||*Pros*||*Cons*||
|Start the test without comms|Not giving false expectation to drivers.
The most low risk.|Test might be invalid.
Might be need to rerun the test again with comms if test result is invalid.|
|Start test with comms - informing this is part of a test and debt limit will be returned again in the future|Better expectation management.
Test will have better result because drivers also aware about when they can pay.|May cause PR or cause driver complaint, high risk.
If in the future we do another test but with lower limit instead, will cause questions from drivers.|
|Start test with comms - without informing the debt limit will be lowered again in the future|Test will have better result because drivers also aware about when they can pay.|Worst expectation management.
May cause PR or cause driver complaint, mild risk.
If in the future we do another test but with lower limit instead, will cause questions from drivers.|

SNS messages can have a maximum size of 256 KB. Larger messages are simply rejected with {{Invalid parameter: Message too long}}.
Reference in the[ AWS docs|https://aws.amazon.com/sns/faqs/#Quotas_and_restrictions]: {{With the exception of SMS messages, Amazon SNS messages can contain up to 256 KB of text data, including XML, JSON and unformatted text.}}

I took a look at some of our messages that happens to exceed the size limit. Even after being processed and with their content being stripped to minimum, their size is still significantly bigger than 256KB (example: [http://kibana.internal/goto/c5667496410ffa0da2552b9cf008e10b|http://kibana.internal/goto/c5667496410ffa0da2552b9cf008e10b])



Recently, Amazon SNS launched a new client library which supports message payloads up to 2 GB ([https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2020/08/amazon-sns-launches-client-library-supporting-message-payloads-of-up-to-2-gb/|https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2020/08/amazon-sns-launches-client-library-supporting-message-payloads-of-up-to-2-gb/]). However, this library is specifically created for Java, so there is no easy way for us to use it.

Perhaps it make sense to „rewrite” this library’s logic for ur Node.js/TS needs, similarly to what other developers have been doing:

[https://medium.com/aspecto/how-to-send-large-sqs-sns-messages-with-node-js-5fc0d85c07e7|https://medium.com/aspecto/how-to-send-large-sqs-sns-messages-with-node-js-5fc0d85c07e7|smart-link]



We could simply upload the message to S3 ([which is already being done for large messages|http://kibana.internal/app/kibana#/doc/logs-nodejs-*/logs-nodejs-2022.09.30/job?id=AYONq5w13G-xa0xfI1N9&_g=(refreshInterval:(display:Off,pause:!f,value:0),time:(from:now-4h,mode:quick,to:now))]) and send new type of SNS event which will contain only data necessary to properly identify the message in any thread AND the link to the file uploaded to S3. 


This would need to be discussed with our further subscribers (CS product).

A note for QA:

Testing of this feature should include basically testing of general chat use cases: creating a chat, sending messages, receiving messages, opening and closing chat, leaving the app and receiving messages, etc. You probably have a set of test cases to test all this.

You should test both cases when the “Chat SDK“ is disabled (the default state) and when it’s enabled as some minor parts related to the initalization were changed in the default implementation as well, so it’s better to make sure nothing is broken there.

In order to enable “Chat SDK“ use a feature flag {{chat_sdk_tier0_enabled}} set to {{true}} either in the Debug drawer menu or in the pre-live admin panel. 

Please keep in mind that the flag value is read on the application initialization phase and as soon as  chat engine is initialized, the implementation will remain the same until the next *restart*. So every time you change the value in the Debug drawer menu, please *kill the app and start it again*.

In order to make sure what implementation the chat engine is currently initialized with, please look for the following messages in the logs:

for the default (the old one) implementation:

{noformat}15:22:54.668 [main] -> Comms - chat   I  Creating a default MQTT controller initializer (null:7)
15:22:54.669 [main] -> Comms - chat   I  Creating a default MQTT controller (null:7){noformat}

or for the “Chat SDK” (the experimental one):

{noformat}15:23:47.573 [main] -> Comms - chat   I  Creating Chat SDK MQTT controller initializer (null:7)
15:23:47.580 [main] -> Comms - chat   I  Creating a Chat SDK MQTT controller (null:7){noformat}

These messages should be printed to the logs somewhere closed to the application start, so they will be on top of the logs.

The discussion around issue types then additional tags, etc, it's a more advanced conversation that I dont feel we can have right now. Why?

* The issue described here and smaller issues are by default generally deprioritised due to the lack of supporting impact assessment
* Impact assessment is not always available because our processes, issue types and tools are designed in such a way to cover super broad topics / issue types. This makes it very difficult to easily break down bigger issues, sub scenarios etc and is mostly dependent on manual deep dive or tagging in a file
* The kind of global change needed to ensure we have a smoother issue tagging system and proper root cause understanding in place is super disruptive, takes time and means that several teams will be involved in the decision-making process. I am 100% for building it from scratch on a new solid foundation, but this needs to be a strong inter-team & leadership collaboration, conversation and a strategic data-driven project.

*1.) Legal Bases:* 
*_Sec 30 DPA 2018:_* 
_Meaning of “competent authority”_

_(1)In this Part, “competent authority” means—_

_(a)a person specified or described in Schedule 7, and_

_(b)any other person if and to the extent that the person has statutory functions for any of the law enforcement purposes._

_(…)_

The NHS Counter Fraud Authority is not  explicit listed in Schedule 7 ([https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2018/12/contents|https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2018/12/contents|smart-link]) Nevertheless it seems that there is an authority named “NHS Counter Fraud Authority” based on the  *NHS Counter Fraud Authority (Investigatory Powers and Other Miscellaneous Amendments) Order 2017 (*[https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2017/960/note/made|https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2017/960/note/made|smart-link]*)*

*Advice:* Bolt works with authorities within the framework of legal requirements, but is also obliged to protect personal data from data subjects. Advice: Request for more detailed notification of the authority status (not listed in schedule 7) and at the same time request for a clear legal basis for the provision of the data (e.g.: legally required obligation to cooperate)

*Schedule 2, Part 1, Section 2, (1)(a) of the Data Protection Act 2018.*

_Crime and taxation: general_

_2(1)The listed GDPR provisions and Article 34(1) and (4) of the_ *_\[_*[_F5_|https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2018/12/schedule/2/part/1#commentary-key-75438dcd3d6caeec4575bd25fb3b15df]_UK GDPR_*_]_* _(communication of personal data breach to the data subject) do not apply to personal data processed for any of the following purposes—_

_(a)the prevention or detection of crime,_

_(b)the apprehension or prosecution of offenders, or_

_(c)the assessment or collection of a tax or duty or an imposition of a similar nature,_

_to the extent that the application of those provisions would be likely to prejudice any of the matters mentioned in paragraphs (a) to (c)._

The investigator states that this request is made in accordance with Schedule 2, Part 1, Section 2, (1)(a) of the Data Protection Act 2018. {noformat}with tunisia_drivers as 
(
	select ic.external_id, ic.type, ebrb.client_id, ebrb.sum_with_vat, ebrb.currency, ebrb.subtype, ebrb.date
	from etl_billing_rides_balance ebrb 
	left join invoicing_client ic on ic.id = ebrb.client_id 
	where ic.country = 'tn' and ic.type in ('Driver', 'Company')
),
month_end_balance as 
(
	select td.external_id, td.type, td.client_id, td.currency, sum(sum_with_vat) as month_end_balance
	from tunisia_drivers td
	where td.date < date('2022-07-01')
	group by 1, 2, 3, 4
	--having month_end_balance < 0
),
collection_after_cutoff as 
(
	select td.external_id, td.type, td.client_id, td.currency, sum(case when sum_with_vat > 0 then sum_with_vat end) as positive_balance_after
	from tunisia_drivers td
	where td.date >= date('2022-07-01')
		and td.date < date('2022-10-01')
	group by 1, 2, 3, 4
),
summary_data as 
(
	select 
	ic."name",
	coalesce(fd.company_name, fc."name", fc2."name") as company_name,
	coalesce(fd.company_id, fc.id) as company_id,
	meb.*, 
	cac.positive_balance_after, 
	least(greatest(-meb.month_end_balance, 0), coalesce(cac.positive_balance_after, 0)) as collection_of_meb
	from month_end_balance meb
	left join collection_after_cutoff cac on cac.client_id = meb.client_id and cac.currency = meb.currency 
	left join fleet_driver fd on fd.id = meb.external_id and meb.type = 'Driver'
	left join fleet_company fc on fc.id = meb.external_id and meb.type = 'Company'
	left join fleet_company fc2 on fc2.id = fd.company_id
	left join invoicing_client ic on ic.id = meb.client_id 
)
select s.name, s.company_name, s.company_id, s.external_id, s.type, s.client_id, s.currency, s.month_end_balance,
s.positive_balance_after, s.collection_of_meb, count(cot2.id) as finished_trips
from summary_data as s
left join company_order_try cot2 on cot2.retry_to_try is null 
	and cot2.state in ('finished') and cot2.driver_id = s.external_id and s.type = 'Driver'
	and cot2.created >= date('2022-07-01')

reply - from Schenker
 

Feedback from my colleagues:

Schenker is in the position that it is important to understand the general legal framework if we talk about freight forwarders liabilities is regulated by international conventions(CMR, Montreal, Hague-Visby), Law Acts and General Conditions set by the countries respective Associations ( General Conditions of ELFA for Carriage of Goods by Road, NSAB).

 

Based on the above the comments are as follows:

 

*Clause 3.3.* - Retention right: Schenker insists in having the right to withhold our goods and even sell them after 2 months in case of payment delays. I don’t think this is proportional and, since it’s a monetary risk for them (not being paid), it should be solved via a monetary mechanism, i.e., interest on delay which is already provided for in the agreement.

 

_This is the basic right to execute right for lien(for example explained as well in CMR Convention) and we surely don’t share the opinion that its not proportional._

 

*Clauses 4.2.5 and 4.2.6* - Schenker’s liability cap for lost goods: Schenker doesn’t seem to agree to deleting liability caps based on Special Drawing Rights (SDR). I suggest that we ask them how many SDR units would apply in each case, as there’s still only a placeholder for that. With that, we can evaluate whether their request is reasonable or not.

 

_Liabilities are very clearly stated in international conventions and they variate per transport mode or warehousing. For example in transportation by road the liability gap is 8,33 SDR per kg._

 

 

*Clause 4.7* – Schenker’s liability cap for transportation services: Schenker insists in limiting their liability in this case to the lowest of the following:  in case of damage or loss, the value of goods per kilogram of the gross weight thereof or (ii) the remuneration for the specific service. This is too low in my opinion and, as previously mentioned, weight-based liability cap doesn’t make sense in our case since we’re mostly talking about Hardware.

 

_In this case BOLT needs to insure the goods and Schenker can provide a solution for this._

 

 

*B. Customs Services Contract*

*Clause 2.3* – Order refusal by Schenker: Schenker suggests that they communicate Bolt of any order refusal within 24h before commencing the services. The original timeline was 5h and we replaced it by 48h. Please let me know if 24h would be acceptable or if we should insist in 48h.

 

 

*Clause 5.1* – Schenker’s liability cap regarding official fines: Schenker is not accepting to cap their liability in case of official fines caused by Schenker’s gross negligence or willful misconduct to the total value of the affected goods. They say it should be a percentage of average taxes and duties value per declaration. I don’t agree. In fact, their liability should be unlimited in this case in my opinion. We are already being flexible by accepting any liability cap at all.

 

_We suggest to agree on cap amount._

* As part of the launch plan, we agreed that during the first year Bolt would cover the cost of capital expenses (courier bags and tablets), and Foodly will cover the rest
* We received those tablets, and we distributed them to providers, some with installments (we made weekly adjustments to their earnings to deduct tablet costs) and some rented out.

* It was later decided not to pay this adjustments to Foodly
* And since we already had issued and declared the invoice with revenue service, we need to write off the loan from accounts receivable, and needed some kind of documental justification to write it off, hence the document currently reviewed by legal.

[~accountid:6012c28a3b1af00069a0c0a7] I think the ADR title is misleading, and I've just fixed it. 

The ADR comes with a preliminary solution for Archiver service, which has to connect to multiple DB schemas. Hence, it raises an exception from the standard config-less procedure, which assumes a service connects only to its own db schema. It opens a backdoor that allows Archiver to work in config-full mode.

It's not about a single user having super power rights; it's about a service whose intrinsic behavior is to connect to multiple DB schemas. 

As we talked about, the first version is intended only for taxify_audit_log, and the ADR tracks that there is a config-less exception for this case.
The next step will be to discuss more and find a complete solution that satisfies all the security concerns.

Now regarding that query, I remember looking at Typeform surveys before (that was specifically for surveys sent to drivers, for example, to drivers registered on the Platform but who have never activated their account - to ask them if they need help, and that implied asking them about their names, email, phone, what kind of help they needed etc) - and these were the +recommendation we gave at the time+:

* It is okay to send such surveys/comms to our *registered drivers* (even if they are not active) *under legitimate interest*.
* It is recommended to *include a short sentence in the survey form* to give the drivers transparency on why we are asking the details and how will we use it. → _“_{color:#4c9aff}_By answering this survey, I acknowledge that the details submitted will be used by Bolt to contact me_{color}_”._
* There should be a *retention time set* for this data that will be collected. Meaning that after the surveys are conducted and drivers have been contacted/helped, the data should be deleted (no fixed time limit, but 3 months would be good).

+The purpose of the surveys that the Business is envisaging here seem different+ however I believe that +scenario 1 and 3+ would be okay, with the same recommendations as listed above. +With scenario 2+, I would be more cautious perhaps, as this could be seen as an incentive to breach their potential duty of confidentiality to our competitors…

*A few things from me.* 

# Your query above makes reference to general terms and conditions but the cross referencing of 4.2 and 1.1 is something I’m confused by. Would you mind linking to me which terms (and which jurisdiction) you are referring to for the purpose of this exercise? For clarity, our UK based terms would reference 1 (a) or 4(b), so let me know if that is what you meant in this instance so I can speak to this for you. 
# The liability the driver holds to the passenger is indeed restricted, this is because we now (following TnC updates) directly contract with the passenger and directly contract with the driver. (See section 10 of General Platform Terms in the online Driver Terms).
# *Passenger Terms and our Liability:* Clause 7 b of our Passenger Terms speaks to our liability to Passengers in saying, Bolt is not responsible to the Passenger for damages, losses or costs relating to their use of our service in a way that isn't permitted under our terms. Then 7c goes on to justify, we are only responsible to Passengers for any damages, losses or costs which result from us not performing our obligations under these Terms *and* which could have been reasonably foreseen by any of the Bolt Parties and you when entering into these Terms. We are therefore performing our obligation under the Bolt>Passenger terms by facilitating this ride-hailing process but we make no guarantee it won’t be error free.
# *Driver Liability to Passengers*: You are correct in your above assessment that ' _the driver does reserve the right to fulfil or reject any offers to fulfil through the driver app_ (this is detailed in section 7a of Driver Terms). _If the driver elects to cancel the trip after confirming it, the contract between Bolt and the passenger for that journey just ensures that the app searches for another driver to complete that trip.'_ In that last sentence though, I would clarify that it is no longer a contract between the Driver and the Passenger, instead we would simply just say *‘the contractual arrangement between Drivers, Bolt and the Passenger for that journey just ensures that the Bolt App searches for another Driver to complete the trip.’*

I do agree with you that there is a lot of confusion to date surrounding this and we will need to treat each matter that comes in with the appropriate nuance according to our terms and when the incident happened. I have reviewed the Terms and Conditions with Ascent Business Centre, it would be helpful to know how many licences to occupy do we have with this provider? Are we really in a position to negotiate? And is there any existing arrangement with Ascent? If so please provide a copy of the terms and conditions agreed to for the previous tenancy.

I have picked up on the following key issues with these Terms and Conditions which is highly favourable to Ascent: 

* *Term:* commencing today with a 3 month term that automatically extends on a rolling basis on 4 January 2023 or on the renewed End Date following an extension if notice to terminate is not provided by Bolt. 
* *Notice period in accordance with the Special Condition:* Bolt would need to provide one months’ written notice in advance of the End Date to terminate this agreement so e.g. if Bolt wants to end the arrangement on 4 January 2023 without it being automatically renewed, it will need to provide notice by 3 December 2022 to ensure that the agreement terminates on 4 January 2023. I am assuming that this arrangement works for Bolt, but please do correct me if I am wrong.
* *Ascent can terminate on or after 4 January 2023 by providing one month’s notice:* this means that after the 4th January 2023, Bolt may be left in a position where it has to find an alternative premises at such short notice. Would this be possible? 
* *Ascent can terminate by providing one week’s written notice in the event of Bolt being in significant breach:* although Ascent’s early termination right in clause 9.1 is only in the event that Bolt commits a significant breach, this is not ideal as Bolt would be required to find alternative premises at very short notice. I am assuming that Markian is happy with this but in future, I would recommend obtaining mutual termination rights.  
* *Repair obligations*: clause 7.2 puts an obligation on us to clean, repair and make good any damage to the area that we demise at our expense. Normally I would push back on this clause as we should not be accepting to repair or to make good damage to a premises that we do not own or have a legal interest in. However, given the urgency of this ticket and that this is an unmanned office and the chances of us causing and repairing damage are low, I would consider this low risk. If we have agreed any works to be undertaken to the premises we are also responsible for removing those works and reinstating the premises identical to as it was before the works were undertaken. I am assuming that Markian is alert to these repair obligations and that we are not carrying out any alteration works to this unmanned office, and therefore consider this to be low risk, but please do bear this obligation in mind if we do decide to make any alterations in future.  
* *Automatic fees renewal:* On each anniversary of the Start Date or renewal, Ascent may carry out reviews of the Licence Fee and Additional Services Charges and can automatically increase the fees under this agreement to the higher of the passing sum or the fee obtainable on a comparable open market agreement. Bolt is liable to pay any subsequent adjustment to the deposit to take account of any increase in the Total Fees following renewal. This is a regular rent review and ideally, we should not be agreeing to rent increases. We should in such circumstances, either have a right to terminate or have a capped amount that the rent can be increased to, but I am assuming that the risk here that Bolt’s rent may be reviewed as often as every three months has been considered but please do correct me if I am wrong.  
* *Indemnity*: Bolt are providing an indemnity for any costs or charges that may arise as a result of non payment of providing Additional Service Charges but as we haven’t signed up to receive any Additional Services, I consider this low risk, but if we do in future, bear in mind that we will be responsible for any costs or charges that may arise from non-payment of Additional Services Charges.
* *Risk assessments:* we are obliged to undertake risk assessments of activities and provide copies to Ascent free of Charge. Do you know what is required in relation to undertaking risk assessments for an unmanned office for Bolt? Given that this is unmanned and a short term tenancy for three months, it may not be applicable and so we can probably leave the wording in clause 7.9 in here for the time being as dormant. But we should know what is required from us in relation to risk assessments so, as an action point for future agreements with Ascent, do raise this with Ascent to determine the extent of our obligations.  
* *Required insurance levels:* we are responsible for maintaining adequate contents insurance, public liability insurance and any other insurances as required by the law and as the business demands but Ascent have not specified insurance levels. Bolt probably has the required insurance levels to cover loss or liabilities for a short term arrangement in any case, but in future, it would be beneficial to know exactly what levels of insurance are required from us to fully determine risk.
* *Business rates:* Bolt is required to register with the appropriate authority for all Business Rates pertaining to the premises from early occupation or commencement to the end of this Agreement and ensure that all Business Rates are paid directly to the appropriate authority, irrespective of the Bolt’s occupation of the premises. Bolt must provide evidence of payment to Ascent. This is our responsibility to pay Business Rates and keep track of it. 
* *Additional fees:* please bear in mind that according to clause 11, we will be penalised by late payment fees, an administration fee of £150 plus VAT, and interest, at a rate of 8% above base rate. There are also additional fees for repair and mail holding. 
* *Guarantor:* I note the guarantor provisions are not relevant, given if it is a short term arrangement, we won’t push for clause 10 to be removed but if this was a more long term arrangement, we should ask for this clause to be removed. 

Really, this licence agreement isn't very favourable to Bolt as it contains rent increase provisions, repair obligations and business rates payments. But given that this is an unmanned office and for a short term, we are able to take a commercial view on the basis that the extent of Bolt’s exposure for rent reviews and repairs is relatively nominal but not normally what we should be agreeing to.

from privacy standpoint it would be also very helpful to see the draft of the communication so I can fully understand what would be the scope of the data disclosure.

In principle, under GDPR sharing driver’s personal data with other drivers wouldn’t be permissible unless we get their prior affirmative consent (which could be also revoked at any time).

However, what also could be considered here in order to conduct this campaign in line with data protection legislation, would be using data that wouldn’t allow for individuals' identification (so the data wouldn’t be deemed personal). Depending on the scope of the data that is intended to be presented in those comms we can propose some anonymisation techniques (such as disclosing only driver’s first name and only in scenarios where there is one than one person with respective name in our database etc).

Hey\!

Here is the summary of the memo and there are some good ideas to consider:

* Reduce the scope of branding restrictions, _e.g.,_ restrictions could apply only to branding of competing platforms and not taxi firms. Also, restrictions apply only while fulfilling a Bolt transportation request (no competitor branding should not be a general requirement to the vehicle).
* Bolt could offer means to cover restricted brands (_e.g_., magnets/ removable stickers). This would help Bolt to argue that branding restrictions do not lead to exclusionary effects in any case as all drivers would be able to swiftly ensure compliance with restrictions and at the same time still use a vehicle rented form a competitor. Moreover, this would enable Bolt to argue that branding restrictions still enable multi-homing. It must be noted that for supporting this argument such means would have to be reasonable and easy to use.
* +Use advertising fees instead of branding restrictions.+ If Bolt was to ask advertising fees from drivers using vehicles with competitors branding to offer services via Bolt, it would soften any anticompetitive effects. Platform would be still open for all vehicles regardless of branding.
* Enforce the branding prohibition via category restrictions. Lastly, even though category restrictions could increase the risk of arguments for discriminatory pricing differences, then it could be an effective means of reducing overall competition law risks. Effect of this would be to ensure that vehicles are not blocked from the platform and hence it could be used to argue that self-preferencing does not have a significant effect on competition. For premium segment cars (for which costs may exceed any revenues arising from offering services under “Basic“ category) use of category restrictions could still lead to a _de facto_ forced exit from the market and cause an existence of an abuse of dominance.

_____

*Some risk of branding restrictions causing leveraging effects on vehicle rental markets thereby amounting to abuse of dominance exists*. This is eventually subject to the factual and economic assessment on whether undertakings offering vehicles for rent can successfully offer vehicle rental for taxi services when the vehicles cannot be used for offering services via Bolt. Presumably they can and there is no abuse, however some risks exist.

Lithuanian competition laws are being interpreted in line with the EU competition rules and practice. Thus, the above findings based on the EU competition rules should also be relevant for Lithuania. In terms of potential intervention, as a general rule Competition Council of the Republic of Lithuania (*“LTCC”*) is less intrusive than ECA. It is rather reluctant to initiate abuse of dominance cases and, even if the case is initiated, the authority tends to close the case if the undertaking at issue accepts the commitments e.g., to modify its behaviour. Having said that we note that Lithuanian competition authority might have a preference to scrutinise activities of Bolt, since the digital economy is one of the priorities for competition authority. Plus, taking into account the structure of the market, the level of dominance of Bolt may be potentially high, thus LTCC might have special interest in Bolt´s activities. 

However, to trigger the proceedings the complainant still must explain the theory of harm and present some evidence that activities at issue cause some negative effect on the market, i.e., the general statements about restriction of freedom to conduct business, etc. usually are not sufficient. Hence, the bar for launching formal investigations in Lithuania is still high (specifically if compared to Estonia). Therefore, if Bolt would follow recommendations on risk mitigation, the probability of formal investigation in Lithuania would be substantially reduced.

*It is not probable that branding restrictions cause foreclosure effects for competitors of Bolt on taxi/ platform services markets (leaving geographical market definition even open)*. Their access to neither input: drivers nor marketing is foreclosed by branding restrictions. Again, final assessment would have to take into account the economic reality.

*Presumably branding restrictions would not amount to abuse of dominance* according to theories of harm of refusal to deal and unfair trading conditions/ discriminatory treatment under EU practice on the driver level.

* We understand that the main aim for applying branding restrictions is the improve the quality of the services offered via platform. From competition law perspective it would be advisable to apply direct objective quality standards. Aim of improving the quality of a service is more easily justifiable in case of any complaints, but measures taken to ensure such end should be proportionate to such means (branding restrictions would likely not be proportionate to ensure quality of service on the platform).
* In the Memorandum economic assessment of the effects of branding restrictions for Bolt´s competitors has been performed (comments are made based on our understanding of the competitive dynamics and previous experiences in similar cases).
* In the Memorandum we have assessed the likely reaction of the national competition authorities based on our earlier experience with said authorities. However, there is no legal certainty for any of the authorities starting/ not starting proceedings primarily due to high interest of competition authorities into the sector (online platforms).

 

As explained above, the challenges to branding prohibition would likely relate to claims that branding restrictions lead to foreclosing input for competitors of Bolt or leveraging taxi/ platform level market power on the rental market. Hence, possible following steps reducing these effects could be taken to mitigate compliance risks.

correct, the four weeks must be guaranteed in any case, before that the customer can also not be charged with the price increase. I would recommend the 6-8 weeks to be on the safe side and prevent consumer lawsuits. Consumers could claim that the email ended up in their spam folder or that they opened the email 5 days later and actually took note of it. A discrepancy of a few days is already sufficient here. That is why I would consider a corresponding buffer and in any case set it at 2 weeks.

Of course, it is everyone's responsibility to check their own e-mail box, but according to German law, correspondence via post is considered delivered only after 3 days after it has been sent. Here, the case law is very much in favour of the consumer.

Hi [~accountid:5e3d437d9749d00c924cb0f5] \!

I understand that this question actually stems from previous discussion also with the PR team. 

So there are several aspects here which I think should be separated to a) communicating with an individual user b) communicating with media/public in general. 

Under GDPR, the actions we take against a user (e.g. block) is considered their personal data. Therefore, as a general rule we cannot share such data directly relating to the person with a third party. So when a user asks what kind of actions were taken, we should refrain from giving out specific information which is deemed as personal data. However, we can confirm or explain indirectly (like you also suggested) that _“in such circumstances Bolt follows internal procedures and takes measures Y.”_  

In cases where we have an inquiry from the media, then there is heightened public interest in a case/situation. This also means that heightened public interest might overweigh the right of privacy. Therefore, more detailed explanation from Bolt may be expected or given. But even then Bolt should refrain from disclosing personal data that is disproportionate and weigh the privacy rights against the public interest in a specific case. 

Liis

Hey Nikola, I appreciate the reply. 

I completely understand the struggle. Honestly, I don’t think CS should even go that deep and manually scan through related users. If you can check just the actual user and look at their volume of finished orders and compare them with current notes, you should probably make better decisions with that. Especially in these cases where the complaint is not verifiable. If the complaint it’s about a delay or cold food, for example, you can see the data on the order page and make a decision based on that. If it’s a complaint about a missing item, not delivered, quality, foreign object in food, or any of those kinds of complaints, CS can sorta already proceed with caution always and verify with calm. There’s no need to rush a decision in a live chat for those kinds of complaints for example. 

My own eater profile for example has 26 manual notes by CS, but I also have over 400 finished orders, so the ratio is fine. The user from this thread has 11 finished orders and literally, all the previous 7 orders have complaints and compensations, so it was possible to flag sooner by seeing that the user was creating a ticket for every order. 

On a higher level, we’re well aware of this lack of information for you guys to handle these kinds of situations and we have plans to improve this flow, however, it will require development from our engineers, and with the current business case, it won’t be prioritized soon, at least not this quarter.

I completely get where you come from, and I understand how helpful it would be to not have to check every profile, or remembering names/pictures.

Progress update [~accountid:5e843e7bcb85aa0c145d4b86] 

* *Prophet without features* achieves 7.3% MAPE (average across cities; 6.7% for top 20 cities, which account for 75% of the GMV in the last 6 months) for daily level price forecasts at the city level. For validation approach, see validation approach below.
* *Prophet using campaign spending.* So far, two partially unsuccessful experiments on how to preprocess spending. They improve the MAPE for about half of the cities, but are not better overall than the Prophet without features.
** Including spending (in the currently performed experiments) doesn’t improve the models for *cities with high price volatility or high GMV*.

!image-20221007-072140.png|width=963,height=79!

* *Next steps:*
** More experiments on the preprocessing of spending, e.g. smoothing (rolling windows).
** Obtain curves of prices at different net rate levels.
** Once we have good results for the accuracy and sensitivity curves, we can
*** Prepare the pipeline.
*** Add enhancements
**** Model competition / Hyperparameter tuning.
**** Add extra regressors, e.g. price per km, price per minut.
* The *validation approach* is a cross-validation for the last 6 months, where for each cutoff a model is trained with all the data until that month, and then the model forecasts the next 30 days. For each cutoff, the MAPE of the next 30 days is computed. This gives 6 MAPEs, which are then averaged, obtaining the final validation metric for that city.

Hi Juste,

thanks for raising this, happy to help. Please see privacy input on this project below:

*Question 1*

Is order to record individuals for marketing purposes you need to obtain the authorisation +prior to the recording both from the driver and the rider+. 

There are 2 options for lawful usage of the recordings:

* *Option 1 - consent for non-paid partnership*. The recording can be used based on individuals consent without any compensation. This option however has a downside, because under GDPR the individual can revoke their consent at any time, which would mean that Bolt would be obliged to remove their image from videos/adds that may have been already produces.
* *Option 2 - using individual’s image based on the contract*. The recording can be used based on the individual's authorisation obtained in exchange for compensation, so the contractual relationship can be established between Bolt and the individual. This option has some advantages, as the authorisation could be obtained for the specific period and cannot be revoked as easily as consent in option 1. Please note that the compensation doesn’t have to be monetary - it can be a voucher/gift card/merchandise.

Could you please look into this and advise which option would be more suitable for the project planned so I can send on appropriate drafts?

And finally please note the following remarks on the IP front:

* make sure not to include any copyrighted content - such as songs we don’t have a right to use (even if e.g. that would be only sung by the driver/rider);
* pay attention to the logos that may appear on the recording (e.g. visible logos on riders' clothing) - those should be blurred.

*Question 2*

If we would like to have verbal conversation about Labas with the drivers, prior question on whether they would like to do that would suffice. If there is however plan to send any marketing communication via e-mail/phone, then recorded prior consent would be required. Please let me know is it the case here.

*Question 3*

Is this NDA full extent of the arrangements planned with Labas? Is there any partnership agreement in place?



BR,

Adriana

I will give my comments to the Article 14 of the agreement here. 

They require that Bolt obtains the written consent of those employees whose personal data (name, surname, e-mail, telephone) is submitted to Interzero for the performance of the contract. I would argue that consent is not necessary since such contact details are provided under the legal basis of performance of the contract and not consent. 

I suggest the following amendment to art 14:

The Partner is obliged to -obtain the Workers' prior written consent- *ensure that there exists a legal basis under applicable data protection regulation,* on the basis of which they authorise INTERZERO to store and use their personal data for the purpose of the performance of the Contract, and to transfer them to third parties. -Upon INTERZERO's request, the Partner shall promptly provide copies of such consents to the Workers.-

*Either way we have to inform our employees that their contact details will be provided to Interzero in regards of the performance of the agreement.

Input in the main ticket. 

The requirement for collecting written consent from employees is unnecessary. There exists another legal basis to rely for the provision of data to the contracting party.

No further action is needed from our side as I understand you’ve already talked to IT as well and the laptops have been disabled and the police have been informed. At this stage, we do not suspect that a third party was able to gain access to any personal or business data.

Currently, there is *no data that indicates a direct correlation* between the *usage and complexity of a process* and the *impact on handling time*. In theory, the common knowledge is that “a long and difficult process” may affect this, however, we don't have an “ideal AHT or TRT” for individual processes. This is a result of not having implemented a data mining framework and tools, that can help us *identify variants and the most common process path*. This also translates into the current issue tagging system, which relies heavily on manual deep-dive. Currently, any process update is nice to have and can be supported by common sense, however, the impact data is biased.

When future developments are available, this can be reopened.

The contract contains some clauses which are insufficient but since this contract is an extension of our agreement with Meniga, we will have to consider whether we can actually request these changes at this stage: 

* *Clause 5.2*: This is more of a practical questions, has the invoicing term been an issue or have we been able to make the payments in due time? In other processes we have seen that 30 days is not always doable for Bolt. If we haven’t had any issues with this then this clause can remain as is. 
* *Clause 7*: The confidentiality term is insufficient, of a very basic nature and doesn't include a survival period. Most importantly we need to include a survival period of 3 years which means that the clause will be valid even when the agreement is terminated. 
* *Clause 8.1*: The agreement includes an automatic extension clause and such clauses should be prevented as far as possible. The extension should only be made if it is agreed upon between both parties in writing. I recommend that this is adjusted so that the parties should agree upon extension 3 months prior to the end date of the agreement otherwise the agreement shall terminate. 
* *Clause 9.1*: The aggregate liability should be limited to the contract value of the contract for a period of the last 12 months, currently it is limited to EUR 100,000. However, since we previously have agreed to this liability cap I think it will be difficult to amend at this stage.  

Please consider the above and revert on our current negotiation position with the company. The confidentiality clause is usually rather easy to implement since it is in the interest of both parties. The other items are more commercial.

Hi Epp,Apologies for the late response. Was traveling all of last week and only now catching up on my backlog. A quick explanation of the account / contract hierarchy in Adyen which I’m hoping will help clarify why the signing entity for the pricing is Bolt Technology and not Bolt Operations:The highest hierarchy is something we call a Company Account. In our back-office it is named Taxify (an old Bolt name we are unable to change). The owner of this main account is Bolt Technology which is also the signing entity for the main Adyen Merchant Agreement.Under the Company Account we have multiple Merchant Accounts - this is the next / second hierarchy level. These Merchant Accounts are owned by multiple Bolt entities depending on the entity who is actually processing payments in that Merchant Account.  So for example Merchant Account TaxifyGLOBAL is owned by Bolt Operations (and for that purpose we have an Affiliate Merchant Agreement with Bolt Operations) while that Merchant Account TaxifyEE is owned by Bolt Services EE Oܠ(and for that purpose we have an Affiliate Merchant Agreement with Bolt Services EE OÜ);The transfer agreement you are pointing at was signed for the purpose of transferring the ownership of a few Merchant Accounts (listed in that signed document last page) from Bolt Technology to Bolt Operations. Therefore the pricing addendum is signed by the owner of the Company Account Taxify = Bolt Technology. *More Details (Ghana)*

|*Ghana*| |
|Biometric data (special category of data)|Not defined in the Data protection act. Nevertheless in the training materials of our external legal counsel (Ghana) they consider genetic and biometric data (for the purpose of unique identification) as special category of data. |Definition biometric data|Not defined in the Data protection act.|
|Legal Bases|Sec 37 (sensitive data) 
* *Consent of the data subject*
* Necessary performance of a right/obligation
* Vital interest|
|Automated decision making|Sec 41: Data subjects are entitled to require at any time by written notice that any decision taken by or on behalf of the data controller which significantly affects that individual is not based solely on the processing by automatic means.  Despite the absence of a notice, where a decision which significantly affects an individual is based solely on that processing  
* the controller shall as soon as reasonably practicable notify the individual that the decision was taken on that basis, and 
* the data subject is entitled to require the controller to reconsider the decision within
 *21 days* after receipt of the notification. 

This does n*ot apply to a decision* made 
* in the course of considering whether to *enter into a contract with the data subject,* 
* with a view to entering into the contract, 
* in the course of the *performance of the contract,* 
* for a purpose authorised by or under an enactment, or in other circumstances prescribed by the Minister.|
|DPIA|The Data Protection Act did not explicitly mention a DPIA. Nevertheless the Data Protection Authority requires one for processing activities with a high risk. *Data Protection Impact Assessments ('DPIA') is a practice that every data controller should commit to*. This is because the Data Protection Act places the DPC in a regulatory position _vis-à-vis_ all data controllers, meaning that data controllers ought to *ensure that compliance monitoring is done at all times to ensure that there are no breaches of the Data Protection Act.* 
The DPA requires that a data controller shall take the necessary steps to secure the integrity of personal data in the possession or control of a person through the adoption ofappropriate, reasonable, technical and organisational measures to prevent:
* loss of, damage to, or unauthorised destruction; and
* unlawful access to or unauthorised processing of personal data.
The Act requires that to give effect to this, the data controller must take reasonable measures to
* *identify reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks t*o personal data under that person's possession or control;
* establish and maintain *appropriate safeguards* against the identified risks;
* *regularly verify that the safeguards* are effectively implemented; and
* ensure that the safeguards are continually updated in response to new risks or deficiencies.|
|Need of a DPA|Yes. A data controller has an obligation to ensure that a data processor who processes personal data for the data controller, establishes and complies with the security measures provided for under the Act. A data processor or a person who processes personal data on behalf of a data controller shall
* process the data only with the prior knowledge or authorisation of the data controller, and
* treat the personal data which comes to the knowledge as confidential.|
|Prime Legislation|The Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843)[https://www.dataprotection.org.gh/data-protection/data-protection-acts-2012|https://www.dataprotection.org.gh/data-protection/data-protection-acts-2012|smart-link]|
|Fines|*No one-stop shop mechanism. The responsible supervisory authority is that in the respective country*
The Data Protection Act provides for sanctions where an individual suffers damage or distress through the contravention by a data controller of the requirements of the Data Protection Act. Such an individual is entitled to compensation from the data controller for damage or distress.

I*ndividual laws also provide that data processing can be restricted/prohibited by supervisory authorities. Furthermore, in the past (Ghana 2021) it was once threatened that the supervisory authority could advise against using the app in a public statement due to data protection concerns.*|

The backfill was performed by running this procedure:



{code:sql}-- ##### UPDATE statement that migrates campaign data #####
-- taxify_delivery_order.campaign_cost_share table ===> taxify_delivery_basket.campaign table

-- UPDATE statement that migrates campaign cost share version and percent in taxify_delivery_basket.campaign table.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS taxify_delivery_basket.update_campaign_cost_share_in_loop;

DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE taxify_delivery_basket.update_campaign_cost_share_in_loop()
BEGIN
    DECLARE v_min_campaign_cost_share_id INT;
    DECLARE v_batch_size INT DEFAULT 200; # TBD with DBAs what is the preferred value here
    DECLARE v_max_campaign_cost_share_id INT DEFAULT 27750548; # campaign cost share created after the deployment

    SELECT MIN(id) INTO v_min_campaign_cost_share_id FROM taxify_delivery_order.campaign_cost_share;

    WHILE v_min_campaign_cost_share_id <= v_max_campaign_cost_share_id DO
            UPDATE taxify_delivery_basket.campaign AS basket_campaign
                JOIN
                (
                    SELECT
                        oc.user_basket_id AS user_basket_id,
                        ocss.cost_share_percent AS order_cost_share_percent,
                        ocss.version AS order_cost_share_version
                    FROM taxify_delivery_order.campaign_cost_share AS ocss
                             INNER JOIN taxify_delivery_order.campaign AS oc
                                        ON ocss.campaign_id = oc.id
                    WHERE ocss.id >= v_min_campaign_cost_share_id
                      AND ocss.id < v_min_campaign_cost_share_id + v_batch_size
                ) AS order_campaign_cost_share

                -- Join is done on the user_basket_id which is the basket identified from schema taxify_delivery_basket
                ON order_campaign_cost_share.user_basket_id = basket_campaign.user_basket_id

                -- Update columns: cost_share_version and cost_share_percentage
            SET
                basket_campaign.cost_share_version = order_campaign_cost_share.order_cost_share_version,
                basket_campaign.cost_share_percentage = order_campaign_cost_share.order_cost_share_percent,
                basket_campaign.last_update = basket_campaign.last_update

            WHERE basket_campaign.id > 0; # needed because of the safe mode

            SET v_min_campaign_cost_share_id = v_min_campaign_cost_share_id + v_batch_size;
        END WHILE;

    SELECT v_min_campaign_cost_share_id;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

CALL taxify_delivery_basket.update_campaign_cost_share_in_loop();

DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS taxify_delivery_basket.update_campaign_cost_share_in_loop;{code}

|Legal Bases|No, there are *no specific provisions regarding the processing of special categories of personal data, including criminal conviction data*. Legal Bases:
* The data subject has given consent to the processing of his or her Personal Data for one or more specific purposes.
* Processing is necessary for the performance of a contract 
* Processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the Controller is subject.
* Processing is necessary in order to protect the vital interests of the data subject or of another natural person.
* Processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official public mandate vested in the controller.
*ATTENTION: The National Information Technology Development Agency ('NITDA') released, on 4 October 2022, the draft Data Protection Bill, 2022 (legal bases for processing are similar to the GDPR). currently it is only a draft and it is not known when the law will come into force*|
|Automated decision making|Section 3.1(7), NDPR Framework Articles 3.2 (xvi) and 5.3.1(f); A Data Subject has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated means, if the decision produces legal effects concerning the data subject or similarly significantly affects him or her.
Automated decision making and profiling are only permitted where:
* necessary for entering into or performing a contract
* *the data subject has given their explicit (i.e. opt-in) consent.*|
|Transparency|*Special transparency requirements* regarding automated decision making|
|DPIA|Section 4.1(5)-(7): The NDPR imposes a general duty on controllers to take into account the risks to the rights and freedoms of natural persons posed by each personal data processing operations.
* Risks (personal data processing system)
* Risks (personal data processing activity)
In assessing the risks to personal data, the following steps are required: 
* Definition of processing activities and its context
* Understanding and evaluation of the impact
* Defining threats and evaluation of the likelihood
* Evaluation of the risk

A DPIA is not compulsory for all processing operations, however, it may be required for the *following types of data processing:*
* {color:#bf2600}*Profiling/Automated decision-making with legal or similar significant effect*{color}
* Systematic monitoring
* {color:#bf2600}*Sensitive data*{color}
* data of vulnerable or differently-abled Data Subject
* When considering the deployment of innovative processes or
application of new technological or organizational solutions|

*More Details (Kenya)*

|*Kenya*| |
|Biometric data (special category of data)|*Sensitive data:* Under the Act, biometric data is  sensitive personal data|
|Definition biometric data|*Biometric data:* This means any personal data resulting from specific technical processing based on physical, physiological, or behavioural characterisation including blood typing, fingerprinting, DNA analysis, earlobe geometry, retinal scanning, and voice recognition.|
|Legal Bases|Sec 45
* *Consent of the data subject*
* personal data which is manifestly made public by the data subject
* establishment, exercise or defence of a legal claim
* vital interests of the data subject|
|Automated decision making|Every data subject has a right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning or significantly affects the data subject. 
This shall not apply where the decision is
* necessary for entering/performing a contract
* authorised by law
* based on consent
*The controller has to inform a data subject when engaging in processing based on automated individual decision making and provide meaningful information about the logic involved;*
He also has to:
* ensure the prevention of errors;
* use appropriate mathematical or statistical procedures;
* put appropriate technical and organisational measures in place to correct inaccuracies and minimise the risk of errors
* process personal data in a way that eliminates discriminatory effects and bias; and
* ensure that a data subject can obtain human intervention and express their point of view.

Hi [~accountid:62bbfa409e6ba34c99365c7c] 

Writing as an internal note, as I’m not quite sure where the actual problem lies here.

I agree with your conclusion that any applicable key terms/conditions/ exclusions should be communicated either in the banner itself, or on a separate page provided it’s no more than 1 click away. General approach for MRK promotion is that we need to be compliant with the regulations (or at least must not unreasonably fail to comply with the applicable rules). 

Proposed: „_Free delivery available from nearby stores on bigger purchases_“ without additional clarification is not sufficient. “Nearby” and “bigger” are relative and misleading terms. Business ought to understand, that in case there is any misinterpretation or misleading information, the consumer will always have the right.   

“Get your groceries delivered in 20-30 minutes. Free delivery available. T&Cs apply.” without actual T&C’s or further clarifications is also not sufficient. 

My thinking here is that we need to give the perimeter/conditions how we define “nearby” (e.g. check your nearby stores in the app); and state the min purchase amount. Should we need T&Cs, then for end-user facing campaigns we have created [a template|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/3921807418/Marketing+agreement+templates#Marketing-campaign-terms-for-end-users], though we may in this case, we may get away more easily by announcing important information on a banner.

I understand that it should be relatively easy to include necessary information on the banner and be compliant. Right? Are there any objective reasons why we should consider otherwise?  

I hope this helps. Also, perhaps Julia could share her experience how she has solved similar problems in the past. 



Br 

Marja-Liisa

Hi everyone\!

Below is the summary re the documents that we now ask from the couriers:

# Photo of an identity document - we need to ask this in order to verify the identity of a courier that is using our platform.
# Health certificate - it is correct that people who work with food should have it. *However,* this requirement applies to *employees* of a companies. Such *companies-employers* then have an obligation to check the health card and maintain the respective records. In case of courier-individual entrepreneurs - they are obliged to obtain the health card with their own money. Bolt as a counterparty of such courier is not obliged to check this.

In any event, an obligation to check the health card lies on the *employer* of a person that is working with food. Bolt is *not an employer* of a courier, we are an information society service provider. *If we check this health card, there might be a reclassification risk since we actually perform an obligation which lies on the employer.*

Therefore, I would say that we can drop the requirement to show us the health card.

*More Details (South Africa)*

|*South Africa*| |
|Biometric data (special category of data)|POPIA defines a separate category of information called 'special personal information' which includes also biometric information.|
|Definition biometric data|'Biometrics' means a technique of personal identification that is based on physical, physiological or behavioural characterisation including blood typing, fingerprinting, DNA analysis, retinal scanning and voice recognition.|
|Legal Bases|Sec 26, 27
* Consent of the data subject
* Necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of a right/obligation
* Comply with an legal obligation
* Historical, statistical or research purpose|
|Automated decision making|Sections 5(g) and 71, POPIA prohibits automated processing of personal information where the data subject will be subjected to a decision which has legal consequences for the data subject or which affects the data subject to a substantial degree. 
*exceptions(Sec 71):*
* Decision has been taken in connection with the conlusion or execution of a contract 
** and the request of the data subject in terms of the contract has been met OR appropriate measures have been taken to protect the data subjects legitimate interests
* Processing activity in governed by a law or a code of conduct in which appropriate measures are specified 
*ALSO a data subject has to have the possibility to questions the decision and the controller has to provide information about the involved logic*|
|Transparency|*Special transparency requirements* regarding automated decision making|
|DPIA|POPIA Regulation 4(b)  Personal Information Impact Assessment ('PIIA')
This process is *mandatory* in terms of POPIA. The aim of conducting a PIIA is to ensure that adequate measures and standards exist in order to comply with POPIA. They also served important secondary role as tangible proof of compliance with POPIA by a responsible party and assist with discharging the responsible party’s obligations of accountability. A PIIA must include:
* describe the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing;
* assess necessity, proportionality and compliance measures;
* identify and assess risks to data subjects; and
* identify any additional measures to mitigate those risks and ensure compliance with the 8 conditions for lawful processing.

Art 57) The controller also hast to obtain prior. authorisation from the regulator prior to any processing if the controller plans to process any unique identifiers of data subjects -
* for a purpose other than the one for which the identifier was specifically intended at collection and
* with the aim of linking the information together with information processed by other controllers.|
|Need of a DPA|Yes. A responsible party must, in terms of a written contract between the responsible party and the operator, ensure that the operator which processes personal information for the responsible party establishes and maintains the security measures as prescribed under POPIA.|
|Prime Legislation|The Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (“POPIA”).[https://inforegulator.org.za/acts/|https://inforegulator.org.za/acts/|smart-link]|
